titleStmt.title: Are We All Amazon Primed? Consumers and the Politics of Platform Power
titleStmt.author: Culpepper
Thelen

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Are We All Amazon Primed? Consumers and the Politics of Platform Power

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: The mechanism that translates market power into political clout, we argue, flows from the appreciation, verging on dependence, that consumers have for the convenience these companies provide.

span.label: platform power
span.quote: This article articulates a distinctive source of political influence of some technology firms, which we call platform power.

span.label: conceptual-analysis
span.term: conceptual-analysis
span.quote: Empirically, we apply this conceptual apparatus to a range of recent, high-profile cases in which platform companies were political protagonists.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Consumer appreciation verging on dependence on platform convenience translates market power into political clout, because politicians anticipate the backlash from depriving constituents of that convenience
span.quote: The mechanism that translates market power into political clout, we argue, flows from the appreciation, verging on dependence, that consumers have for the convenience these companies provide.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Which of a person's identities is made salient shifts their regulatory preferences: priming the citizen identity produces sociotropic preferences, priming the consumer identity produces a narrow focus on self-interest
span.quote: Priming citizen identity can lead to more sociotropic preferences, while priming consumer identity can lead to a narrower focus on individual self-interest.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Platform power operates automatically in politicians' minds as anticipated political fallout, not as fear of disinvestment or job loss
span.quote: The power these companies wield operates not through politician’s fear of the pain that these firms can visit upon the economy so much as the anticipated political fallout to which overeager regulators would expose themselves by messing with the infrastructure of people’s lives.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A TERM IS COINED IN ONE SENTENCE AND GIVEN A STRUCTURAL DEFINITION IN THE NEXT: this article articulates a distinctive source of political influence of some technology firms, **WHICH WE CALL PLATFORM POWER**. The coinage is announced as the article's contribution, so the word arrives already carrying the claim it was invented to make
span.quote: This article articulates a distinctive source of political influence of some technology firms, which we call platform power.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: AND THE DEFINITION IS A STRUCTURAL POSITION RATHER THAN A PROPERTY OF THE FIRM: platform power **INHERES IN COMPANIES OF ECONOMIC SCALE THAT PROVIDE THE TERMS OF ACCESS** through which large numbers of consumers access goods, services, and information. What the term denotes is a place in a structure - who controls the terms of access - not a size, a sector, or a behaviour
span.quote: Platform power inheres in companies of economic scale that provide the terms of access through which large numbers of consumers access goods, services, and information.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE TERM IS THEN DEFINED BY WHAT IT IS NOT, RULING OUT THE FIELD'S TWO STANDARD MECHANISMS BY NAME: firms with platform power benefit from a deference from policymakers, but this deference **IS NOT PRIMARILY A FUNCTION OF DIRECT INFLUENCE THROUGH LOBBYING OR CAMPAIGN CONTRIBUTIONS**, **NOR DOES IT COME FROM THE THREAT OF DISINVESTMENT**. The new construct is positioned by excluding the two things political economy already had words for
span.quote: Firms with platform power benefit from a deference from policymakers, but this deference is not primarily a function of direct influence through lobbying or campaign contributions, nor does it come from the threat of disinvestment.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE THRESHOLD FOR THE TERM IS SET DELIBERATELY BELOW THE LEGAL ONE, IN A PARENTHETICAL: platform firms that achieve **A CERTAIN ECONOMIC SCALE - WHICH NEED NOT REACH MONOPOLY PROPORTIONS -** benefit from the direct relationship they enjoy to a large number of consumers **WHO RELY ON THE PLATFORM AS IT BECOMES INTEGRATED INTO THE FABRIC OF THEIR DAILY LIVES**. The concept is built to apply where antitrust does not reach, and the gap is stated rather than left to be noticed
span.quote: We argue that platform firms that achieve a certain economic scale – which need not reach monopoly proportions – benefit from the direct relationship they enjoy to a large number of consumers who rely on the platform as it becomes integrated into the fabric of their daily lives.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A PRIOR DISTINCTION IS ATTRIBUTED TO THE SCHOOL THAT BUILT IT, AS SCAFFOLDING: **MARXIST SCHOLARS BUILT SOME OF THE SCAFFOLDING FOR THESE MODERN DEBATES BY DISTINGUISHING BETWEEN THE INSTRUMENTAL AND STRUCTURAL POWER OF BUSINESS**. The two inherited terms are named, dated and credited before the paper argues that neither covers its case
span.quote: Marxist scholars built some of the scaffolding for these modern debates by distinguishing between the instrumental and structural power of business (e.g., Miliband 1969, Poulantzas 1972, Block 1980).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: AND THE INHERITED VOCABULARY IS DECLARED INSUFFICIENT RATHER THAN WRONG: however, **IT IS NOT AT ALL CLEAR THAT THE TOOLS AND STRATEGIES OF INSTRUMENTAL POWER REPRESENT THE PRINCIPAL FORM OF INFLUENCE THESE COMPANIES WIELD**. The older term is left standing and denied primacy, which is a different move from refuting it
span.quote: However, it is not at all clear that the tools and strategies of instrumental power represent the principal form of influence these companies wield.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: AN ASSUMPTION IS ATTRIBUTED TO THREE RIVAL APPROACHES AT ONCE, AND IT IS THE ASSUMPTION THE PAPER DENIES: **LEGAL APPROACHES THAT STRESS MONOPOLY CONTROL ALONE, JUST AS INSTRUMENTAL AND STRUCTURAL POWER APPROACHES, ASSUME THAT ECONOMIC INCENTIVES ARE FOREMOST IN THE MINDS OF POLICYMAKERS** who are considering adopting regulations that constrain business. One premise is extracted from three literatures and named as the thing they share
span.quote: Legal approaches that stress monopoly control alone, just as instrumental and structural power approaches, assume that economic incentives are foremost in the minds of policymakers who are considering adopting regulations that constrain business.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: `BY DEFINITION` IS USED TO CONCEDE A GENERAL TRUTH AND THEN SET IT ASIDE: **CONSUMERS ARE BY DEFINITION IMPORTANT TO ANY CAPITALIST ENTERPRISE**, but the relationship to today's dominant platforms **GOES BEYOND FAMILIAR MODELS OF CONSUMER LOYALTY OR COST-BASED CHOICE**. The phrase marks what does not need arguing so that the contrast can carry the argument
span.quote: Consumers are by definition important to any capitalist enterprise, but the relationship to today’s dominant platforms goes beyond familiar models of consumer loyalty or cost-based choice.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: AND THE PAPER REPLACES ONE OF ITS OWN WORDS MID-ARGUMENT, SAYING WHICH ONE IT MEANS: once these firms reach scale, **IT IS NOT SO MUCH CONSUMER LOYALTY THAT INSPIRES THE COALITION BETWEEN USERS AND PLATFORM AS CONSUMER DEPENDENCE**. Two candidate terms for one relationship, and the substitution is performed in the open rather than by drifting usage
span.quote: Once these firms reach scale, it is not so much consumer loyalty that inspires the coalition between users and platform as consumer dependence.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: DEPENDENCE IS OPERATIONALISED BY A BEHAVIOURAL CONTRAST CONCRETE ENOUGH TO CHECK: **CONSUMERS LOVE LEGO BUT THEY ARE NOT DEPENDENT ON THE COMPANY IN THE SAME WAY** that they are dependent on Amazon, **WHICH ACTUALLY ALLOWS THEM TO ORDER THEIR LEGOS WITHOUT HAVING TO CHANGE OUT OF THEIR PAJAMAS**. Affection and dependence are separated by what the firm lets you avoid doing, and the test is a scene rather than a measure
span.quote: By contrast, consumers love Lego but they are not dependent on the company in the same way that they are dependent on, say, Amazon, which actually allows them to order their Legos without having to change out of their pajamas.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE DIFFERENCE FROM EARLIER DOMINANT FIRMS IS LOCATED IN THE CONNECTION, NOT THE SIZE: **UNLIKE PREVIOUS GENERATIONS OF LARGE COMPANIES ON WHICH THE BROADER ECONOMY CAME TO DEPEND**, such as railways or utility companies, today's largest platforms enjoy **A TIGHT, EVEN INTIMATE, CONNECTION TO THEIR USERS**. The comparison class is named - railways, utilities - so the novelty claim can be checked against it
span.quote: Unlike previous generations of large companies on which the broader economy came to depend, such as railways or utility companies, today’s largest platforms enjoy a tight, even intimate, connection to their users.

span.label: The phenomenon is too recent for systematic testing of the paper's propositions.
span.quote: The recency of the rise of platform power as a phenomenon limits our ability to test these propositions systematically.

span.label: The survey evidence on preferring company self-regulation is American only; the authors lack comparable data elsewhere.
span.quote: Although we lack the data to know if this specific impulse exists in public opinion outside the United States, the general popularity and trust of consumers for technology companies that we have documented in this section is an international phenomenon, one that serves the political interests of large platform firms in a variety of countries around the world.

span.label: The assumed consumer preference against regulation is a simplification the authors concede.
span.quote: Our treatment of consumer preferences for regulation is admittedly somewhat stylized: if a regulation does good for consumers without having any effect on their ability to enjoy the conveniences delivered by platform innovation, there is in theory no reason consumers should oppose regulation.

span.label: The concept of priming - that individuals hold multiple identities whose salience can be cued, thereby shifting their political preferences - is imported to explain when consumers defend or abandon platform firms.
span.quote: Our theoretical position draws on the priming literature in social science, which posits that individuals have multiple identities, the salience of which can influence their political preferences on a given political issue.

span.label: The permissive-consensus model of EU public opinion is borrowed as the analogy for how consumer support licenses platform firms until salient issues break it.
span.quote: The orientation of today’s consumers with respect to companies enjoying platform power can perhaps best be made by analogy to what Hooghe and Marks (2009) called the permissive consensus in public opinion.

span.label: platform power
span.term: platform power
span.quote: In common with Lindblom’s (1982) punishing recoil mechanism, platform power is largely automatic – it happens in the minds of politicians. The difference, though, is that in the case of platform power, the potential loss is not disinvestment or job loss.

span.label: structural power
span.term: structural power
span.quote: In common with Lindblom’s (1982) punishing recoil mechanism, platform power is largely automatic – it happens in the minds of politicians. The difference, though, is that in the case of platform power, the potential loss is not disinvestment or job loss.

span.label: quiet politics
span.term: quiet politics
span.quote: Representatives of business have traditionally engaged in forum-shopping, to find the arena in which the tools of quiet politics are most effective. The preferred arena of conflict for business is typically a regulatory conference room rather than a public parliamentary hearing (Culpepper 2011).

span.label: platform power - NOT A THING ANYONE DOES: it is 'LARGELY AUTOMATIC - IT HAPPENS IN THE MINDS OF POLITICIANS', an anticipated reaction rather than an act of lobbying, disinvestment or campaign spending. A power exercised by nobody, which is what makes it hard to observe and easy to deny
span.quote: In common with Lindblom’s (1982) punishing recoil mechanism, platform power is largely automatic – it happens in the minds of politicians. The difference, though, is that in the case of platform power, the potential loss is not disinvestment or job loss.

span.label: the resource that carries the power - CONSUMERS, NOT MONEY OR JOBS: firms 'benefit from THE TACIT ALLEGIANCE OF CONSUMERS, who can prove a formidable source of opposition to regulations that threaten these platforms'. The asset is an alliance the firm does not have to organise and cannot fully control
span.quote: Companies with platform power instead benefit from the tacit allegiance of consumers, who can prove a formidable source of opposition to regulations that threaten these platforms.

span.label: builds-on → Hooghe and Marks (2009), permissive consensus
span.quote: The orientation of today’s consumers with respect to companies enjoying platform power can perhaps best be made by analogy to what Hooghe and Marks (2009) called the permissive consensus in public opinion.

span.label: builds-on → Naoi and Kume (2015) on priming consumer identity and trade preferences
span.quote: Empirical support for this proposition can be found in the area of international trade preferences, where Naoi and Kume (2015) show that the priming of consumer identities in Japan raised support for free trade by up to 9 percent, compared to a control group.

span.label: platform power —distinct-from→ structural power
span.term: platform power
structural power
span.note: differs in: WHAT THE THREATENED LOSS IS. Both work the same way - 'In common with Lindblom's (1982) punishing recoil mechanism, PLATFORM POWER IS LARGELY AUTOMATIC - IT HAPPENS IN THE MINDS OF POLITICIANS.' The difference is the content of the anticipated punishment: 'in the case of platform power, THE POTENTIAL LOSS IS NOT DISINVESTMENT OR JOB LOSS.' Two powers with one mechanism and different currencies, which is why a measure built for disinvestment threat would score platform firms at zero · strength of the relation: 0.9
span.quote: In common with Lindblom’s (1982) punishing recoil mechanism, platform power is largely automatic – it happens in the minds of politicians. The difference, though, is that in the case of platform power, the potential loss is not disinvestment or job loss.

span.label: platform power —contrasted-with→ quiet politics
span.term: platform power
quiet politics
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8 — THE ARENA IS PART OF THE STRATEGY AND PLATFORM FIRMS INVERT THE USUAL ONE. Business normally forum-shops toward the venue where quiet politics works - 'The preferred arena of conflict for business is typically A REGULATORY CONFERENCE ROOM RATHER THAN A PUBLIC PARLIAMENTARY HEARING.' The paper's claim is that platform companies sometimes prefer the public arena instead, because their power runs through consumers rather than through informational advantage.
span.quote: Representatives of business have traditionally engaged in forum-shopping, to find the arena in which the tools of quiet politics are most effective. The preferred arena of conflict for business is typically a regulatory conference room rather than a public parliamentary hearing (Culpepper 2011).

span.label: The political deference dominant platform firms enjoy comes from the tacit allegiance of consumers rather than from lobbying, campaign contributions or the threat of disinvestment.
span.quote: Firms with platform power benefit from a deference from policymakers, but this deference is not primarily a function of direct influence through lobbying or campaign contributions, nor does it come from the threat of disinvestment.

span.label: Market power alone does not produce platform power: economic dominance is necessary but must be combined with a direct consumer relationship.
span.quote: Market power is a necessary but not sufficient condition for platform power.

span.label: Because they can mobilise a loyal consumer base, platform firms are more willing than other big businesses to fight openly in public and legislative arenas rather than in the quiet politics of regulatory conference rooms.
span.quote: According to this logic, platform companies are more likely than nonplatform companies to engage in broad-based political campaigns, pitting their popularity against those of their opponents.

span.label: The Snowden revelations split the consumer-platform alliance by exposing platforms as conduits of state surveillance, and the resulting public anger strengthened the EU's data protection regulation.
span.quote: That is, the Snowden revelations drove a wedge into the alliance between platforms and consumers by revealing to consumers that there was a hidden cost of their reliance on information platforms. The ensuing public outrage contributed to a significant strengthening of the GDPR (Rossi 2016).

span.label: Danish unions defeated Uber by reframing it as a tax and welfare-state question, appealing to people as taxpaying citizens instead of convenience-seeking consumers.
span.quote: The Danish unions were able to reframe the issue of Uber’s entry into the market – appealing to voters as (tax-paying) citizens rather than (convenience-loving) consumers – a winning strategy, since it cast Uber as being premised on a business model that was at odds with the preservation of a national system that works only if everyone is paying their fair share.

span.label: Platforms whose users are local voters (Uber) win political protection that platforms whose users are non-resident visitors (Airbnb) cannot, so Airbnb has faced heavier city-level regulation and has moved its lobbying to the EU level.
span.quote: Politicians are more likely to bend to platforms where the platform’s users are their own voters, which helps to explain why mayors across a range of cities in different countries have imposed more regulations on Airbnb than Uber.

span.label: Where consumer and platform interests coincide, as with the harsh labour practices behind fast cheap Amazon delivery, no political mobilisation follows because consumers are themselves implicated in the practice.
span.quote: Consumers are unlikely to mobilize around this issue since they themselves are complicit in it.

span.label: The paper predicts that a platform losing consumer confidence will lose regulatory battles even when its share price and market share are untouched.
span.quote: platform companies that suffer substantial losses of consumer confidence are likely to suffer regulatory losses, regardless of whether their share price or market share is affected.

span.label: Courts and competition authorities, being insulated from consumer pressure, are named as the most likely durable check on platform power, rather than consumers themselves.
span.quote: Indeed, we have suggested that courts and competition authorities may pose the biggest threats to platform power, precisely because of their relative insulation from consumer pressure.

span.label: platform power
span.term: platform power
span.quote: Platform power inheres in companies of economic scale that provide the terms of access through which large numbers of consumers access goods, services, and information.

span.label: platform power (what confers it)
span.term: platform power (what confers it)
span.quote: But for those that do achieve such scale and influence, the direct connection to the consumer confers a distinctive form of power.

span.label: permissive consensus
span.term: permissive consensus
span.quote: The permissive consensus held that public opinion across member states of the European Union (EU) was broadly positive toward the European project, and that this positive orientation gave political leaders some freedom to craft new institutional deals

span.label: alignment vs. divergence of consumer and platform interests in public debate
span.term: alignment vs. divergence of consumer and platform interests in public debate
span.quote: In the first part of this section, we examine temporal and spatial variation in the success of platform power, depending on the way in which public debates highlighted the convergence or divergence of interests between platforms and their users.

span.label: loss of consumer confidence in a platform firm
span.term: loss of consumer confidence in a platform firm
span.quote: And when the only thing keeping regulators from imposing new rules is the fear of consumer backlash, that translates into this empirical expectation: platform companies that suffer substantial losses of consumer confidence are likely to suffer regulatory losses, regardless of whether their share price or market share is affected.

span.label: political effectiveness / regulatory outcomes for platform firms
span.term: political effectiveness / regulatory outcomes for platform firms
span.quote: Putting the consumer-platform alliance in the analytical foreground helps to explain variations in the political strategies and observed political effectiveness of platform companies around the world.

span.label: 74 percent — Share of respondents in the 2018 Edelman Trust Barometer trusting the technology sector to do what is right, the highest of any industry
span.quote: the technology sector stood at 74 percent in 2018. No other industry had a score higher than 62 percent that year

span.label: 39 vs. 56 percent — Americans wanting the US government to restrict false information online versus wanting tech companies to do it
span.quote: As shown in Table 3, only 39 percent of Americans thought the US government should restrict the flow of false information online, while in response to otherwise identical question wording, 56 percent of Americans thought technology companies should perform these functions.

span.label: $13 million — Amazon's 2017 US lobbying spending, up from $2.5 million five years earlier
span.quote: Amazon alone increased its spending on American lobbying to roughly $13 million in 2017, as opposed to equivalent spending of $2.5 million 5 years earlier (Lynch 2017).

span.label: 56 percent — Americans naming Facebook as the least trusted tech company just after the Cambridge Analytica scandal, against 5 percent for Google
span.quote: One poll of American adults, taken just after outbreak of the scandal in early 2018, showed that 56 percent of people named Facebook as the tech company they trusted least; the next least trusted was Google, with 5 percent.

span.label: 2.4 million views — Reach of the Danish union's anti-Uber video campaign, in a country of 5.7 million people
span.quote: The Danish-language films went viral, achieving over 2.4 million views in a country of 5.7 million people.

span.label: five of the top six — Places held by platform companies in YouGov's 2018 global brand health rankings
span.quote: In the 2018 global brand health rankings created by the polling firm YouGov, platform companies took five of the top six places (table 1).

span.label: $45 million — Cost of Facebook's publicity campaign for Free Basics in India
span.quote: Facebook retaliated with a publicity campaign that cost $45 million and featured billboards promoting “digital equality.”

p.note: The full text of this article is not redistributable, so it is not included here. Every tag above carries the exact sentence it was made from, quoted under fair quotation. The article itself is at https://doi.org/10.1177/0010414019852687.
